You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /luxon.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

     2	
     3	## Invalid DateTimes
     4	
     5	One of the most irritating aspects of programming with time is that it's possible to end up with invalid dates. This is a bit subtle: barring integer overflows, there's no count of milliseconds that don't correspond to a valid DateTime, but when working with calendar units, it's pretty easy to say something like "June 400th". Luxon considers that invalid and will mark it accordingly.
     6	
     7	Unless you've asked Luxon to throw an exception when it creates an invalid DateTime (see more on that below), it will fail silently, creating an instance that doesn't know how to do anything. You can check validity with `isValid`:
     8	
     9	```js
    10	> var dt = DateTime.fromObject({ month: 6, day: 400 });
    11	dt.isValid //=> false
    12	```
    13	
    14	All of the methods or getters that return primitives return degenerate ones:
    15	
    16	```js
    17	dt.year; //=>  NaN
    18	dt.toString(); //=> 'Invalid DateTime'
    19	dt.toObject(); //=> {}
    20	```
    21	
    22	Methods that return other Luxon objects will return invalid ones:
    23	
    24	```js
    25	dt.plus({ days: 4 }).isValid; //=> false
    26	```
    27	
    28	## Reasons a DateTimes can be invalid
    29	
    30	The most common way to do that is to over- or underflow some unit:
    31	
    32	- February 40th
    33	- 28:00
    34	- -4 pm
    35	- etc
    36	
    37	But there are other ways to do it:
    38	
    39	```js
    40	// specify a time zone that doesn't exist
    41	DateTime.local().setZone("America/Blorp").isValid; //=> false
    42	
    43	// provide contradictory information (here, this date is not a Wedensday)

190	### keepLocalTime
   191	
   192	Generally, it's best to think of the zone as a sort of metadata that you slide around independent of the underlying count of milliseconds. However, sometimes that's not what you want. Sometimes you want to change zones while keeping the local time fixed and instead altering the timestamp. Luxon supports this:
   193	
   194	```js
   195	var local = DateTime.local();
   196	var rezoned = local.setZone("America/Los_Angeles", { keepLocalTime: true });
   197	
   198	local.toString(); //=> '2017-09-13T18:36:23.187-04:00'
   199	rezoned.toString(); //=> '2017-09-13T18:36:23.187-07:00'
   200	
   201	local.valueOf() === rezoned.valueOf(); //=> false
   202	```
   203	
   204	If you find that confusing, I recommend just not using it. On the other hand, if you find yourself using this all the time, you are probably doing something wrong.
   205	
   206	## Accessors
   207	
   208	Luxon DateTimes have a few different accessors that let you find out about the zone and offset:
   209	
   210	```js
   211	var dt = DateTime.local();
   212	
   213	dt.zoneName; //=> 'America/New_York'
   214	dt.offset; //=> -240
   215	dt.offsetNameShort; //=> 'EDT'
   216	dt.offsetNameLong; //=> 'Eastern Daylight Time'
   217	dt.isOffsetFixed; //=> false
   218	dt.isInDST; //=> true
   219	```
   220	
   221	Those are all documented in the [DateTime API docs](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html).
   222	
   223	## DST weirdness
   224	
   225	Because our ancestors were morons, they opted for a system wherein many governments shift around the local time twice a year for no good reason. And it's not like they do it in a neat, coordinated fashion. No, they do it whimsically, varying the shifts' timing from country to country (or region to region!) and from year to year. And of course, they do it the opposite way south of the Equator. This is all a tremendous waste of everyone's energy and, er, time, but it is how the world works and a date and a time library has to deal with it.
   226	
   227	Most of the time, DST shifts will happen without you having to do anything about it and everything will just work. Luxon goes to some pains to make DSTs as unweird as possible. But there are exceptions. This section covers them.
   228	
   229	### Invalid times
   230	
   231	Some local times simply don't exist. The Spring Forward DST shift involves shifting the local time forward by (usually) one hour. In my zone, `America/New_York`, on March 12, 2017 the millisecond after 1:59:59.999 is 3:00:00.000. Thus the times between 2:00:00.000 and 2:59:59.000, inclusive, don't exist in that zone. But of course, nothing stops a user from constructing a DateTime out of that local time.
   232	
   233	If you create such a DateTime from scratch, the missing time will be advanced by an hour:
   234	
   235	```js
   236	DateTime.local(2017, 3, 12, 2, 30).toString(); //=> '2017-03-12T03:30:00.000-04:00'
   237	```
   238	
   239	You can also do date math that lands you in the middle of the shift. These also push forward:
   240	
   241	```js
   242	DateTime.local(2017, 3, 11, 2, 30)
   243	  .plus({ days: 1 })
   244	  .toString(); //=> '2017-03-12T03:30:00.000-04:00'
   245	DateTime.local(2017, 3, 13, 2, 30)
   246	  .minus({ days: 1 })
   247	  .toString(); //=> '2017-03-12T03:30:00.000-04:00'
   248	```
   249	
   250	### Ambiguous times
   251	
   252	Harder to handle are ambiguous times. During Fall Back, some local times happen twice. In my zone, `America/New_York`, on November 5, 2017 the millisecond after 1:59:59.000 became 1:00:00.000. But of course there was already a 1:00 that day, one hour before before this one. So if you create a DateTime with a local time of 1:30, which time do you mean? It's an important question, because they correspond to different moments in time.
   253	
   254	However, Luxon's behavior here is undefined. It makes no promises about which of the two possible timestamps the instance will represent. Currently, its specific behavior is like this:
   255	
   256	```js
   257	DateTime.local(2017, 11, 5, 1, 30).offset / 60; //=> -4
   258	DateTime.local(2017, 11, 4, 1, 30).plus({ days: 1 }).offset / 60; //=> -4
   259	DateTime.local(2017, 11, 6, 1, 30).minus({ days: 1 }).offset / 60; //=> -5
   260	```
   261	
   262	In other words, sometimes it picks one and sometimes the other. Luxon doesn't guarantee the specific behavior above. That's just what it happens to do.
   263	
   264	If you're curious, this lack of definition is because Luxon doesn't actually know that any particular DateTime is an ambiguous time. It doesn't know the time zones rules at all. It just knows the local time does not contradict the offset and leaves it at that. To find out the time is ambiguous and define exact rules for how to resolve it, Luxon would have to test nearby times to see if it can find duplicate local time, and it would have to do that on every creation of a DateTime, regardless of whether it was anywhere near a real DST shift. Because that's onerous, Luxon doesn't bother.
   265	
   266	### Math across DSTs
   267	
   268	There's a whole [section](math.html) about date and time math, but it's worth highlighting one thing here: when Luxon does math across DSTs, it adjusts for them when working with higher-order, variable-length units like days, weeks, months, and years. When working with lower-order, exact units like hours, minutes, and seconds, it does not. For example, DSTs mean that days are not always the same length: one day a year is (usually) 23 hours long and another is 25 hours long. Luxon makes sure that adding days takes that into account. On the other hand, an hour is always 3,600,000 milliseconds.
   269	
   270	An easy way to think of it is that if you add a day to a DateTime, you should always get the same time the next day, regardless of any intervening DSTs. On the other hand, adding 24 hours will result in DateTime that is 24 hours later, which may or may not be the same time the next day. In this example, my zone is `America/New_York`, which had a Spring Forward DST in the early hours of March 12.
   271	
   272	```js
   273	var start = DateTime.local(2017, 3, 11, 10);
   274	start.hour; //=> 10, just for comparison
   275	start.plus({ days: 1 }).hour; //=> 10, stayed the same
   276	start.plus({ hours: 24 }).hour; //=> 11, DST pushed forward an hour
   277	```
   278	
   279	## Changing the default zone
   280	
   281	By default, Luxon creates DateTimes in the system's local zone. However, you can override this behavior globally:
   282	
   283	```js
   284	Settings.defaultZoneName = "Asia/Tokyo";
   285	DateTime.local().zoneName; //=> 'Asia/Tokyo'
   286	
   287	Settings.defaultZoneName = "utc";
   288	DateTime.local().zoneName; //=> 'UTC'
   289	
   290	// you can reset by setting to 'local'
   291	
   292	Settings.defaultZoneName = "local";
   293	DateTime.local().zoneName; //=> 'America/New_York'
   294	```
